reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
clinicalPearls: Occurs when blood is diverted away from an ischaemic myocardial territory towards an adjacent bed with lower vascular resistance, worsening rather than relieving regional ischaemia.
Vasodilator stress agents such as adenosine, regadenoson and dipyridamole can provoke steal by maximally dilating normal vessels while a stenosis limits flow reserve in the dependent territory.
Coronary-subclavian steal arises after use of an internal mammary artery graft when a proximal subclavian stenosis reverses flow, drawing blood from the myocardium to the arm.
Suspect coronary-subclavian steal in a bypass patient with recurrent angina, an inter-arm blood pressure difference and arm claudication or a diminished ipsilateral pulse.
Collateral-dependent myocardium supplied through vessels from a bed with a proximal stenosis is particularly vulnerable to the steal effect.
Symptoms typically emerge during exertion or pharmacological vasodilatation, when the resistance gradient between beds is greatest.
Management targets the culprit lesion, most often percutaneous revascularisation of a subclavian stenosis in the coronary-subclavian variant.
Duplex ultrasound and angiography demonstrating reversed internal mammary or subclavian flow confirm the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Coronary steal reflects the redistribution of limited coronary blood flow governed by differences in vascular resistance between adjacent perfusion beds. When a territory is supplied through a fixed proximal stenosis or through collaterals, its distal arterioles are already near-maximally dilated to preserve resting flow, leaving little reserve. Administration of a potent arteriolar vasodilator, or physiological demand, further lowers resistance in the normally perfused neighbouring bed, so flow preferentially follows the path of least resistance and is diverted away from the dependent, resistance-exhausted territory, deepening its ischaemia. In the coronary-subclavian variant a proximal subclavian obstruction reverses flow in an internal mammary artery graft, siphoning coronary blood into the upper limb.
additionalDifferentials: subclavian steal syndrome affecting the vertebrobasilar circulation
peripheral arterial disease of the upper limb
additionalInvestigations: duplex ultrasonography of the subclavian and internal mammary arteries
myocardial perfusion imaging with vasodilator stress
computed tomographic or magnetic resonance angiography of the arch and grafts
coronary physiology assessment with fractional flow reserve
twelve-lead electrocardiogram during induced or exertional symptoms
redFlags: recurrent angina after internal mammary artery bypass grafting
significant inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference
ischaemia or haemodynamic deterioration provoked by vasodilator stress testing
arm claudication or absent pulse with concurrent chest pain
reference.prognosis: Outcome is favourable once the responsible lesion is corrected, with revascularisation of a subclavian stenosis typically abolishing angina in the coronary-subclavian variant; untreated, the diverted myocardial supply predisposes to recurrent ischaemia.
pitfalls: Measuring blood pressure in only one arm and missing the inter-arm gradient that signals subclavian stenosis.
Interpreting stress-induced ischaemia as fixed disease progression without considering a steal mechanism.
Overlooking a proximal subclavian lesion in a symptomatic internal mammary graft recipient.
Assuming symptoms reflect graft failure when flow reversal is the true cause.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ACC/AHA guideline on the management of patients with peripheral artery disease
management: Correct the responsible lesion definitively: revascularise a proximal subclavian stenosis by angioplasty and stenting or surgical bypass in coronary-subclavian steal to abolish angina
Revascularise a flow-limiting coronary stenosis driving collateral-dependent steal by percutaneous intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting
Avoid provocative vasodilator stress agents such as adenosine, regadenoson and dipyridamole where they may worsen steal, using alternative testing
Provide anti-ischaemic medical therapy for symptom control while definitive treatment is arranged
Institute secondary prevention with risk-factor modification, antiplatelet and statin therapy
Coordinate care through a cardiology and vascular surgery multidisciplinary team
Monitor for recurrent ischaemia and escalate as untreated steal predisposes to further ischaemic events
